To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the use of remotely observed river water level data from satellite altimetry can improve model calibration when combined with GRACE data and readily available river geometry information, and that increasing the number virtual stations used for calibration can considerably improve the spatial split sample validation.

the use of remotely observed river water levels from multiple virtual stations in combination with GRACE observations can be used to identify model parameter sets in data scarce regions when river geometry data are available.

satellite altimetry observations from virtual stations combined with global high resolution terrain and GRACE data have the potential to identify feasible parameter sets of a distributed hydrological model in a poorly gauged basin, and that the use of river geometry information extracted directly from Google Earth can significantly improve the model performance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a distributed hydrological model for the data scarce Luangwa River basin in Zambia.
the question whether altimetry data are useful in identifying parameter sets for hydrological models.
the question whether remotely sensed river water levels from satellite altimetry missions can be used to identify feasible model parameters in the absence of discharge observations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the results of this study show that the use of satellite altimery observations can be a promising alternative to discharge measurements for the calibration and identification of model parameters in data scarce regions.
the use of remotely sensing data in combination with hydrological modelling can be very useful in data sparse regions to obtain a better understanding of the water balance.
the use of satellite altimetric river water levels in combination with GRACE data to identify feasible model parameters in a data scarce region is feasible and promising.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

satellite data from multiple sources and different scales can be combined to improve hydrological model parameter selection in regions with limited data availability, thereby improving model performance and reliability in data scarce regions and ungauged river basins.
altimetry observations can provide valuable information to constrain hydrological model parameters, especially when used with other information such as river geometry and GRACE.
the combination of GRACE data and altimetry observations can be used to identify feasible parameter sets for a distributed hydrological model.
The main takeaway from our work is that

satellite altimetry observations are valuable for model calibration and can be used to identify feasible model parameters in data scarce basins when combined with other remotely sensed data such as GRACE.
altimetry observations can be a valuable data source for the calibration of hydrological models in data scarce regions if the right approach is chosen.

the use of altimery observations for model parameter identification can be highly beneficial in data scarce regions and that the use of satellite altimery data in hydrology should be considered as an alternative to traditional methods.
